claim: DNMT1 function is regulated by O-GlcNAcylation, a protein modification that is sensitive to glucose levels.
source: The DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1 is vital for genomic maintenance of DNA methylation. We report here that DNMT1 function is regulated by O-GlcNAcylation, a protein modification that is sensitive to glucose levels, and that elevated O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 from high glucose environment leads to alterations to the epigenome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Elevated O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 from high glucose environment leads to alterations to the epigenome.
source: We report here that DNMT1 function is regulated by O-GlcNAcylation, a protein modification that is sensitive to glucose levels, and that elevated O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 from high glucose environment leads to alterations to the epigenome.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: S878 is the major residue that is O-GlcNAcylated on human DNMT1.
source: Using mass spectrometry and complementary alanine mutation experiments, we identified S878 as the major residue that is O-GlcNAcylated on human DNMT1.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and alanine mutation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-S878 results in an inhibition of methyltransferase activity.
source: Functional studies in human and mouse cells further revealed that O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-S878 results in an inhibition of methyltransferase activity, resulting in a general loss of DNA methylation that preferentially occurs at partially methylated domains (PMDs).
evidence: This is supported by functional studies using DNA methyltransferase activity assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-S878 results in a general loss of DNA methylation that preferentially occurs at partially methylated domains (PMDs).
source: Functional studies in human and mouse cells further revealed that O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-S878 results in an inhibition of methyltransferase activity, resulting in a general loss of DNA methylation that preferentially occurs at partially methylated domains (PMDs).
evidence: This is supported by nanopore sequencing data showing preferential loss of methylation at PMDs (Figure 4).

claim: Loss of methylation from O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 corresponds with an increase in DNA damage and apoptosis.
source: This loss of methylation corresponds with an increase in DNA damage and apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by γ-H2A.X staining for DNA damage and PI staining for cell death shown in Figure 5.

claim: Protein O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic and reversible post-translational modification that attaches a single O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine to serine or threonine residues.
source: Protein O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic and reversible post-translational modification that attaches a single O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine to serine or threonine residues (Hart et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hart et al., 1996.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is modulated by two O-GlcNAc cycling enzymes, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA), that respond to metabolic signals.
source: It is modulated by two O-GlcNAc cycling enzymes, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA), that respond to metabolic signals (Hart et al., 2007; Slawson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hart et al., 2007 and Slawson et al., 2010.

claim: Increased concentrations of UDP-GlcNAc that are observed in conditions of excess glucose lead to a general increase in protein O-GlcNAcylation.
source: Increased concentrations of UDP-GlcNAc that are observed in conditions of excess glucose lead to a general increase in protein O-GlcNAcylation (Walgren et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Walgren et al., 2003.

claim: Obesogenic diets have elevated protein O-GlcNAcylation in various human cell types, including liver cells, lymphocytes, and immune cells.
source: Obesogenic diets, furthermore, have elevated protein O-GlcNAcylation in various human cell types, including liver cells (Guinez et al., 2011), lymphocytes (Torres and Hart, 1984), and immune cells (de Jesus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of proteins can influence the function and/or stability of the targeted proteins.
source: As with other post-translational modifications, O-GlcNAcylation of proteins can influence the function and/or stability of the targeted proteins (Shin et al., 2018; Yang and Qian, 2017b).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Shin et al., 2018 and Yang and Qian, 2017b.

claim: Thousands of proteins are targets for O-GlcNAcylation, including many epigenetic regulatory proteins.
source: Thousands of proteins are targets for O-GlcNAcylation, including many epigenetic regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The O-GlcNAcylation of TET family proteins alters their activity, localization, and targeting.
source: For example, the O-GlcNAcylation of TET family proteins alters their activity, localization, and targeting (Chen et al., 2013; Ito et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: All DNA methyltransferases have been shown to be O-GlcNAcylated.
source: While all DNA methyltransferases have been shown to be O-GlcNAcylated (Boulard et al., 2020), the functional consequences of this have not been previously investigated.
evidence: This is cited from Boulard et al., 2020.

claim: The functional consequences of O-GlcNAcylation of DNA methyltransferases have not been previously investigated.
source: While all DNA methyltransferases have been shown to be O-GlcNAcylated (Boulard et al., 2020), the functional consequences of this have not been previously investigated.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: DNMT1 is imperative for maintaining DNA methylation patterns during replication.
source: Among the DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) family of proteins, DNMT1 is imperative for maintaining DNA methylation patterns during replication (Bestor and Ingram, 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Bestor and Ingram, 1983.

claim: DNMT1 is a modular protein with several domains necessary for interacting with cofactors, including the BAH1 and BAH2 domains.
source: DNMT1 is a modular protein with several domains necessary for interacting with cofactors, including the BAH1 and BAH2 domains (Maresca et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Maresca et al., 2015 and Ren et al., 2018.

claim: The stability and function of DNMT1 have been shown to be regulated through post-translational modifications, including acetylation, phosphorylation, and methylation.
source: The stability and function of DNMT1 have been shown to be regulated through post-translational modifications, including acetylation, phosphorylation, and methylation (Scott et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Scott et al., 2014.

claim: Partially methylated domains (PMDs) were originally identified in cultured cell lines.
source: Partially methylated domains (PMDs), large domains with a loss of DNA methylation, were originally identified in cultured cell lines (Lister et al., 2009) and subsequently found to be a characteristic of cancer cells (Berman et al., 2011; Brinkman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Lister et al., 2009.

claim: PMDs are a characteristic of cancer cells.
source: Partially methylated domains (PMDs), large domains with a loss of DNA methylation, were originally identified in cultured cell lines (Lister et al., 2009) and subsequently found to be a characteristic of cancer cells (Berman et al., 2011; Brinkman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Berman et al., 2011 and Brinkman et al., 2019.

claim: PMDs have been detected in non-cancerous healthy tissues, where they are associated with late replication loci.
source: PMDs have also been detected in non-cancerous healthy tissues, where they are associated with late replication loci (Hansen et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hansen et al., 2010 and Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: PMDs are generally thought to arise from a lack of fidelity in maintenance methylation.
source: While PMDs are generally thought to arise from a lack of fidelity in maintenance methylation (Decato et al., 2020), the mechanisms responsible for the establishment of PMDs have remained unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Decato et al., 2020.

claim: The mechanisms responsible for the establishment of PMDs have remained unclear.
source: While PMDs are generally thought to arise from a lack of fidelity in maintenance methylation (Decato et al., 2020), the mechanisms responsible for the establishment of PMDs have remained unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Inhibition of OGA increased global levels of O-GlcNAc while inhibition of OGT decreased global levels of O-GlcNAc.
source: As expected, immunoblots of cellular lysate with an antibody recognizing pan-O-GlcNAc (RL2) reveal that inhibition of OGA increased global levels of O-GlcNAc while inhibition of OGT decreased global levels of O-GlcNAc (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TMG treatment increases O-GlcNAc of DNMT1 while OSMI treatment decreases O-GlcNAc.
source: Immunoblots with O-GlcNAc antibodies revealed that TMG treatment increases O-GlcNAc of DNMT1 while OSMI treatment decreases O-GlcNAc (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: DNMT1 is O-GlcNAcylated in Hep3B cells, HepG2 cells, and B-cell-derived lymphocytes.
source: In addition to Hep3B cells, we found that DNMT1 is O-GlcNAcylated in HepG2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and B-cell-derived lymphocytes, indicating that DNMT1 is O-GlcNAcylated across various cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The total amount of protein O-GlcNAcylation was increased with high glucose treatment.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Andrews et al., 2000), the total amount of protein O-GlcNAcylation was increased with high glucose treatment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Global protein O-GlcNAcylation was induced with high concentrations of sucrose, albeit to a lower extent than with glucose.
source: Global protein O-GlcNAcylation was also induced with high concentrations of sucrose, albeit to a lower extent than with glucose (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: High glucose treatment increased the O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1.
source: As with the analysis of total protein, high glucose treatment increased the O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High sucrose treatment increased the O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1.
source: High sucrose treatment also increased the O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The increased O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 with high glucose and sucrose treatment was also observed in HepG2 cells.
source: The increased O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 with high glucose and sucrose treatment was also observed in HepG2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The changes in O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 from glucose treatment were not influenced by alterations in the activity of OGT or OGA.
source: The changes in O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 from glucose treatment were not influenced by alterations in the activity of OGT or OGA as we observed the enzymatic activity of OGT or OGA was not significantly changed by glucose treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), consistent with previous results (Seo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and is consistent with previous results.

claim: An increase in O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 occurs in primary cells (PBMCs) with increased glucose levels.
source: Consistent with our observations in Hep3B cells, we observed an increase in O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 with increased glucose levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data from PBMCs shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Combining high glucose condition with OGA inhibition by TMG resulted in a further increase in O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1.
source: Combining the high glucose condition with OGA inhibition by TMG resulted in a further increase in O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Liver samples from mice fed an obesogenic high-fat/high-sucrose (HF/HS) diet displayed an increase in total O-GlcNAcylation.
source: These samples displayed an increase in total O-GlcNAcylation in liver samples from HF/HS fed mice (Figure 1D) as well as increased O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data from mouse liver samples shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Liver samples from mice fed an obesogenic high-fat/high-sucrose (HF/HS) diet displayed increased O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1.
source: These samples displayed an increase in total O-GlcNAcylation in liver samples from HF/HS fed mice (Figure 1D) as well as increased O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data from mouse liver samples shown in Figure 1D.

claim: OGTSite identified 16 candidate O-GlcNAc modified sites on human DNMT1.
source: OGTSite, which uses experimentally verified O-GlcNAcylation sites to build models of substrate motifs, identified 16 candidate O-GlcNAc modified sites on human DNMT1 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using OGTSite.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that S878, which is located on the bromo-associated homology (BAH1) domain of DNMT1, is O-GlcNAcylated.
source: Peptide analyses revealed that S878, which is located on the bromo-associated homology (BAH1) domain of DNMT1 is O-GlcNAcylated (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 2.

claim: S878 is conserved through vertebrates to Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Analysis of the evolutionary conservation of DNMT1 sequence (details in 'Materials and methods') revealed that S878 is conserved through vertebrates to Arabidopsis thaliana (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Three previously unreported phosphorylated residues were detected (T208, S209, and S1122).
source: Three previously unreported phosphorylated residues were also detected (T208, S209, and S1122) (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplementary files 2 and 3.

claim: Loss of threonine and serine at positions T158 and S878 respectively resulted in a loss of O-GlcNAcylation.
source: Loss of threonine and serine at positions T158 and S878 respectively resulted in a loss of O-GlcNAcylation, indicating that these two residues are required for O-GlcNAcylation, with the DNMT1-S878A and DNMT1-T158A/S878A mutant resulting in >50% reduction of O-GlcNAcylation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by alanine mutation experiments and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: T158 (near the PCNA binding domain) and S878 (within the BAH1 domain) are the O-GlcNAcylated residues of DNMT1.
source: These results indicate that T158 (near the PCNA binding domain) and S878 (within the BAH1 domain) are the O-GlcNAcylated residues of DNMT1.
evidence: This is concluded from the alanine mutation experiments.

claim: The BAH domains of DNMT1 are known to be necessary for DNA methyltransferase activity.
source: The BAH domains of DNMT1 are known to be necessary for DNA methyltransferase activity (Gong et al., 2021; Yarychkivska et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Gong et al., 2021 and Yarychkivska et al., 2018.

claim: High glucose/TMG treatment reduced the activity of DNMT1.
source: Intriguingly, high glucose/TMG treatment reduced the activity of DNMT1 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DNA methyltransferase activity assay data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a dose-dependent inhibition of the DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1 with increasing glucose concentrations in PBMCs.
source: We observed a striking dose-dependent inhibition of the DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by DNA methyltransferase activity assay data from PBMCs shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Liver samples of mice fed an HF/HS diet showed a decreased activity of DNMT1 compared to chow-fed mice.
source: Lastly, we examined the activity of DNMT1 in the liver samples of mice fed an HF/HS diet, which showed a decreased activity of DNMT1 (Figure 3C) compared to chow-fed mice.
evidence: This is supported by DNA methyltransferase activity assay data from mouse liver samples shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1-S878A is not inhibited by high glucose/TMG treatment.
source: Compared to the DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1-WT (Myc-DNMT1-WT), the DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1-S878A (Myc-DNMT1-S878A) is not inhibited by high glucose/TMG treatment (Figure 3D), indicating that O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-S878 is directly involved in the inhibition of methyltransferase activity.
evidence: This is supported by DNA methyltransferase activity assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-S878 is directly involved in the inhibition of methyltransferase activity.
source: Compared to the DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1-WT (Myc-DNMT1-WT), the DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1-S878A (Myc-DNMT1-S878A) is not inhibited by high glucose/TMG treatment (Figure 3D), indicating that O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-S878 is directly involved in the inhibition of methyltransferase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the S878A mutant is not inhibited by high glucose/TMG treatment.

claim: The DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1-T158A is inhibited by high glucose/TMG treatment in a manner similar to DNMT1-WT.
source: In contrast, the DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1-T158A (Myc-DNMT1-T158A) is inhibited by high glucose/TMG treatment in a manner similar to DNMT1-WT (Myc-DNMT1-WT), indicating that O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-T158 does not affect its DNA methyltransferase activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by DNA methyltransferase activity assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-T158 does not affect its DNA methyltransferase activity.
source: In contrast, the DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1-T158A (Myc-DNMT1-T158A) is inhibited by high glucose/TMG treatment in a manner similar to DNMT1-WT (Myc-DNMT1-WT), indicating that O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1-T158 does not affect its DNA methyltransferase activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the T158A mutant is inhibited similarly to WT.

claim: DNMT1-S878 can be phosphorylated.
source: A previous phospho-proteomic analysis revealed that DNMT1-S878 can be phosphorylated (Zhou et al., 2013), but the functional consequences of this have not been investigated.
evidence: This is cited from Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: The DNMT1-S878D phosphomimetic mutant did not have loss of DNA methyltransferase activity with high glucose/TMG treatment.
source: With treatment this phospho-mimetic mutant did not have loss of DNA methyltransferase activity, indicating that O-GlcNAcylation of S878 but not phosphorylation of S878 is leading to loss of methyltransferase activity of DNMT1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by DNA methyltransferase activity assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of S878 but not phosphorylation of S878 is leading to loss of methyltransferase activity of DNMT1.
source: With treatment this phospho-mimetic mutant did not have loss of DNA methyltransferase activity, indicating that O-GlcNAcylation of S878 but not phosphorylation of S878 is leading to loss of methyltransferase activity of DNMT1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the phosphomimetic mutant does not show loss of activity.

claim: Treatment with high glucose/TMG leads to a loss of DNA methylation in a manner comparable with a DNA methylation inhibitor, GSK-3484862.
source: Comparison of DNA methylation under high glucose/TMG and treatment with DNA methylation inhibitors (5-aza or GSK-3484862 [Azevedo Portilho et al., 2021]; details in 'Materials and methods') revealed that treatment leads to a loss of DNA methylation in a manner comparable with a DNA methylation inhibitor, GSK-3484862 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by global DNA methylation LINE-1 assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The methylation loss resulting from treatment with high glucose/TMG was not apparent in the DNMT1-S878A mutant.
source: The methylation loss resulting from treatment with high glucose/TMG was not apparent in the DNMT1-S878A mutant, further demonstrating that O-GlcNAcylation of S878 within DNMT1 directly affects DNA methylation activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by global DNA methylation LINE-1 assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of S878 within DNMT1 directly affects DNA methylation activity.
source: The methylation loss resulting from treatment with high glucose/TMG was not apparent in the DNMT1-S878A mutant, further demonstrating that O-GlcNAcylation of S878 within DNMT1 directly affects DNA methylation activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the S878A mutant does not show methylation loss.

claim: There was no correlation between phosphorylation of DNMT1 S878 and DNA loss of methylation loss under high glucose/TMG conditions.
source: When we assessed methylation with the phosphor-mimetic mutant (DNMT1-S878D), there was no correlation between phosphorylation of DNMT1 S878 and DNA loss of methylation loss under high glucose/TMG conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by global DNA methylation LINE-1 assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Changes in DNMT1 under hyperglycemia do not appear to impact its nucleocytoplasmic localization.
source: However, changes in DNMT1 under hyperglycemia do not appear to impact its nucleocytoplasmic localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: A comparison of the methylation profiles in DNMT1-WT cells revealed a global loss of methylation in high glucose compared to control.
source: A comparison of the methylation profiles in these cells revealed a global loss of methylation in high glucose compared to control (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4A, 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the DNMT1-S878A mutant, there was no appreciable decrease in DNA methylation by high glucose.
source: Conversely, for the DNMT1-S878A mutant, there was no appreciable decrease in DNA methylation by high glucose (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of S878 of DNMT1 leads to a global loss of DNA methylation.
source: These results collectively indicate that O-GlcNAcylation of S878 of DNMT1 leads to a global loss of DNA methylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of WT and S878A mutant methylation profiles.

claim: DNA methylation changes induced by O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 revealed a preferential loss of DNA methylation at liver cancer PMDs.
source: Examination of DNA methylation changes induced by O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 revealed a preferential loss of DNA methylation at liver cancer PMDs (Li et al., 2016) that was not observed in S878A mutant cells (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: PMDs are relatively gene poor and harbor mostly lowly transcribed genes.
source: PMDs have several defining features, including being relatively gene poor and harboring mostly lowly transcribed genes (Decato et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Decato et al., 2020.

claim: Regions that lose methylation in high glucose conditions are largely gene-poor.
source: We stratified the genome in terms of gene density and transcription rate (see 'Materials and methods' for details) and found that regions that lose methylation in high glucose conditions are largely gene-poor (Figure 4D) and contain lowly transcribed genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Regions that lose methylation in high glucose conditions contain lowly transcribed genes.
source: We stratified the genome in terms of gene density and transcription rate (see 'Materials and methods' for details) and found that regions that lose methylation in high glucose conditions are largely gene-poor (Figure 4D) and contain lowly transcribed genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: PMDs have been linked to regions of late replication associated with the nuclear lamina.
source: PMDs have furthermore been linked to regions of late replication associated with the nuclear lamina (Brinkman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Brinkman et al., 2019.

claim: In DNMT1-WT cells, late replication domains preferentially lose DNA methylation in high glucose/TMG conditions compared to early replication domains.
source: In DNMT1-WT cells, late replication domains preferentially lose DNA methylation in high glucose/TMG conditions compared to early replication domains (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data in relation to replication timing shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Loss of methylation at late replication domains was not observed in DNMT1-S878A mutant cells.
source: This loss of methylation was not observed in DNMT1-S878A mutant cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: One of the major functions of DNA methylation in mammalian genomes is the repression of repetitive elements.
source: One of the major functions of DNA methylation in mammalian genomes is the repression of repetitive elements (Edwards et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Edwards et al., 2017.

claim: Many chromatin proteins involved in the repression of TEs are capable of being O-GlcNAcylated.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that many chromatin proteins involved in the repression of TEs are capable of being O-GlcNAcylated (Boulard et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Boulard et al., 2020.

claim: High glucose conditions resulted in methylation loss at TEs in a manner similar to the nonrepetitive fraction of the genome.
source: We found that high glucose conditions resulted in methylation loss at TEs in a manner similar to the nonrepetitive fraction of the genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), with a more dramatic loss of methylation at LINEs and LTRs compared to SINE elements (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is a more dramatic loss of methylation at LINEs and LTRs compared to SINE elements under high glucose conditions.
source: We found that high glucose conditions resulted in methylation loss at TEs in a manner similar to the nonrepetitive fraction of the genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), with a more dramatic loss of methylation at LINEs and LTRs compared to SINE elements (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Evolutionarily recent TEs are more likely to lose methylation than older elements in a variety of systems.
source: Given that evolutionarily recent TEs are more likely to lose methylation than older elements in a variety of systems (Almeida et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2020), we examined the methylation status of two younger subfamilies, LTR12C (Hominoidea) and HERVH-int (Catarrhini) elements (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Almeida et al., 2022 and Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: HERVH-int elements show a loss of methylation similar to the rest of the genome.
source: While HERVH-int elements show a loss of methylation similar to the rest of the genome, LTR12C elements do not lose methylation in the same manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that they are protected from the loss of methylation.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: LTR12C elements do not lose methylation in the same manner as the rest of the genome, suggesting that they are protected from the loss of methylation.
source: While HERVH-int elements show a loss of methylation similar to the rest of the genome, LTR12C elements do not lose methylation in the same manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that they are protected from the loss of methylation.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and is a speculative interpretation.

claim: ZFP57 and ZNF605 demonstrate binding to a significant number of LTR12C elements present in liver cancer PMDs.
source: ZFP57 and ZNF605 demonstrate binding to a significant number of LTR12C elements present in liver cancer PMDs (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), suggesting that binding of these KZFPs could maintain the methylation at LTR12Cs.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of ChIP-exo data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Binding of ZFP57 and ZNF605 could maintain the methylation at LTR12Cs.
source: ZFP57 and ZNF605 demonstrate binding to a significant number of LTR12C elements present in liver cancer PMDs (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), suggesting that binding of these KZFPs could maintain the methylation at LTR12Cs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the binding data.

claim: Evolutionarily recent elements in general are less likely to lose methylation than older elements.
source: Stratifying all TEs by evolutionary age (Storer et al., 2021) and examining the methylation changes induced by O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 for each clade revealed that evolutionarily recent elements in general are less likely to lose methylation than older elements (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of nanopore sequencing data stratified by evolutionary age shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: Genes with hypomethylated promoters are involved in apoptosis and oxidative stress response pathways.
source: Pathway analysis (see 'Materials and methods' for details) revealed that genes with hypomethylated promoters are involved in apoptosis and oxidative stress response pathways (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of genes with hypomethylated promoters shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Apoptosis agonist proteins (cleaved-caspase3 and phopho-p53 [S15]) are increased by high glucose treatment.
source: Examination of apoptosis-related proteins using an apoptosis proteome array revealed that apoptosis agonist proteins (cleaved-caspase3 and phopho-p53 [S15]) are increased and antagonistic proteins (pro-caspase3, surviving, and claspin) are decreased by high glucose treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis proteome array data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Apoptosis antagonistic proteins (pro-caspase3, surviving, and claspin) are decreased by high glucose treatment.
source: Examination of apoptosis-related proteins using an apoptosis proteome array revealed that apoptosis agonist proteins (cleaved-caspase3 and phopho-p53 [S15]) are increased and antagonistic proteins (pro-caspase3, surviving, and claspin) are decreased by high glucose treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis proteome array data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only cIAP-1 is increased in the high glucose-treated DNMT1-S878A mutant cells.
source: Intriguingly, only cIAP-1 is increased in the high glucose-treated DNMT1-S878A mutant cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis proteome array data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: High glucose-induced generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) has been shown to result in increased cell death.
source: High glucose-induced generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) has been shown to result in increased cell death (Allen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Allen et al., 2005.

claim: Increased ROS has been shown to result in upregulation of DNMT1.
source: Increased ROS has furthermore been shown to result in upregulation of DNMT1 (He et al., 2012; O'Hagan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from He et al., 2012 and O'Hagan et al., 2011.

claim: The levels of ROS were increased upon treatment with 25 mM glucose with TMG in both DNMT1-WT and DNMT1-S878A.
source: The levels of ROS were increased upon treatment with 25 mM glucose with TMG in both DNMT1-WT and DNMT1-S878A (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by DCFH-DA fluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DNA damage indicated by levels of γ-H2A.X was reduced in high glucose/TMG-treated DNMT1-S878A cells compared to WT cells despite high ROS levels.
source: Interestingly, DNA damage indicated by levels of γ-H2A.X was reduced in high glucose/TMG-treated DNMT1-S878A cells compared to WT cells despite high ROS levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by γ-H2A.X immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DNA oxidative damage was reduced in high glucose-treated DNMT1-S878A cells compared to WT cells.
source: This also reduced DNA oxidative damage in high glucose-treated DNMT1-S878A cells compared to WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by 8-OHdG assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: DNA damage induced by low glucose with GSK-3484862 treatment suggests that DNA hypomethylation is associated with increased DNA damage.
source: Furthermore, DNA damage induced by low glucose with GSK-3484862 treatment suggests that DNA hypomethylation is associated with increased DNA damage (Figure 5—figure supplement 4; Azevedo Portilho et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by 8-OHdG assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Cell death was prominently increased in the high glucose-treated DNMT1-WT cells but suppressed in the DNMT1-S878A mutants.
source: Finally, examination of propidium iodide (PI) levels revealed that cell death was prominently increased in the high glucose-treated DNMT1-WT cells but suppressed in the DNMT1-S878A mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ROS-induced DNA damage under hyperglycemic conditions is partially mitigated by DNA methylation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that ROS-induced DNA damage under hyperglycemic conditions is partially mitigated by DNA methylation; elevated O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 coinciding with DNA methylation loss is associated with more ROS-induced DNA damage and increased cell death.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the combined results.

claim: Elevated O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 coinciding with DNA methylation loss is associated with more ROS-induced DNA damage and increased cell death.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that ROS-induced DNA damage under hyperglycemic conditions is partially mitigated by DNA methylation; elevated O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 coinciding with DNA methylation loss is associated with more ROS-induced DNA damage and increased cell death.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the combined results.

claim: Extracellular metabolic stress and cell fate are linked through epigenetic regulation.
source: These results indicate that extracellular metabolic stress and cell fate are linked through epigenetic regulation.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The function of the Bromo-Adjacent Homology (BAH) domain is to mediate association of DNMT1 with replication foci during S phase to maintain methylation.
source: The function of the Bromo-Adjacent Homology (BAH) domain is to mediate association of DNMT1 with replication foci during S phase to maintain methylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the BAH domain function.

claim: The BAH-deleted form of DNMT1 was unable to maintain DNA methylation genome-wide or in IAP retrotransposons and major satellite DNA.
source: The BAH-deleted form of DNMT1 was unable to maintain DNA methylation genome-wide or in IAP retrotransposons and major satellite DNA, commonly densely methylated sequences (Yarychkivska et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Yarychkivska et al., 2018.

claim: The DNMT1 S878F mutation results in hypomethylation of the HBG promoter region.
source: In addition, the DNMT1 S878F mutation results in hypomethylation of the HBG promoter region (Gong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Gong et al., 2021.

claim: Direct O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 disrupts the BAH1 domain, thereby suppressing the function of DNMT1.
source: Our findings suggest that the direct O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 disrupts the BAH1 domain, thereby suppressing the function of DNMT1.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism based on the study's findings.

claim: PMDs have been suggested to be associated with mitotic dysfunction.
source: PMDs have been observed in both healthy and disease cells and have been suggested to be associated with mitotic dysfunction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PMDs.

claim: Models for how PMDs are established remain incomplete.
source: However, models for how these domains are established remain incomplete (Decato et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge cited from Decato et al., 2020.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 at S878 due to increased glucose levels can inhibit the function of DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1, resulting in loss of methylation and establishment of PMDs.
source: The results presented here suggest an additional layer whereby O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 at S878 due to increased glucose levels can inhibit the function of DNA methyltransferase activity of DNMT1, resulting in loss of methylation and establishment of PMDs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation and proposed mechanism based on the study's findings.

claim: High glucose conditions have previously been reported to lead to an increase in nuclear 25-hydroxycholesterol, which induces lipid accumulation and activates DNMT1.
source: High glucose conditions have previously been reported to lead to an increase in nuclear 25-hydroxycholesterol, which induces lipid accumulation and activates DNMT1 (Allen et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Allen et al., 2005 and Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The activity of DNMT1 gradually increases with glucose concentrations.
source: Our results are consistent with the activity of DNMT1 gradually increasing with glucose concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-dependent DNA methyltransferase activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increased activity of DNMT1 associated with glucose treatment is directly inhibited by O-GlcNAcylation within DNMT1.
source: This trend is reversed, however, upon TMG treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the increased activity of DNMT1 associated with glucose treatment is directly inhibited by O-GlcNAcylation within DNMT1.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the reversal of the trend with TMG treatment.

claim: Dysregulation of O-GlcNAcylation, driven by increased blood glucose levels in diabetes or the Warburg effect in cancer cells, has been shown to play a crucial role in disease progression.
source: Dysregulation of O-GlcNAcylation, driven by increased blood glucose levels in diabetes (Ling and Rönn, 2019) or the Warburg effect in cancer cells, has been shown to play a crucial role in disease progression (Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009), which results in an increase in intracellular protein O-GlcNAcylation (Hart et al., 2007; Hart et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation acts as a molecular switch that can modulate protein function in response to nutrient changes and serve as a molecular sensor for specific cellular signals.
source: O-GlcNAcylation acts as a molecular switch that can modulate protein function in response to nutrient changes and serve as a molecular sensor for specific cellular signals (Vaidyanathan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Vaidyanathan et al., 2014 and Yang et al., 2017a.

claim: Perturbations in the activity of O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA) enzymes, as well as alterations in posttranslational modifications, can disrupt protein functions vital for cell survival and contribute to metabolic reprogramming.
source: Perturbations in the activity of O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA) enzymes (Wells et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2003), as well as alterations in posttranslational modifications, can disrupt protein functions vital for cell survival and contribute to metabolic reprogramming (Shin et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: The increased levels of O-GlcNAcylation observed in most diabetic patients and tumors suggest its potential utility as a biomarker.
source: The increased levels of O-GlcNAcylation observed in most diabetic patients and tumors (de Queiroz et al., 2014) suggest its potential utility as a biomarker.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on established knowledge.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 impairs its methyltransferase function, leading to global loss of DNA methylation and aberrant activity of transposable elements.
source: Our study highlights the impact of O-GlcNAcylation on DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), revealing its role in modulating DNA methylation. O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 impairs its methyltransferase function, leading to global loss of DNA methylation and aberrant activity of transposable elements.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes have been linked to epigenetic changes that alter gene regulation.
source: Metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes have been linked to epigenetic changes that alter gene regulation (Ling and Rönn, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Ling and Rönn, 2019.

claim: There is a general increase in protein O-GlcNAcylation in hyperglycemia conditions.
source: It has previously been established that there is a general increase in protein O-GlcNAcylation in hyperglycemia conditions (Vasconcelos-Dos-Santos et al., 2018) and several epigenetic regulatory factors have been shown to have increased O-GlcNAcylation under high glucose conditions (Bauer et al., 2015; Etchegaray and Mostoslavsky, 2016; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Several epigenetic regulatory factors have been shown to have increased O-GlcNAcylation under high glucose conditions.
source: It has previously been established that there is a general increase in protein O-GlcNAcylation in hyperglycemia conditions (Vasconcelos-Dos-Santos et al., 2018) and several epigenetic regulatory factors have been shown to have increased O-GlcNAcylation under high glucose conditions (Bauer et al., 2015; Etchegaray and Mostoslavsky, 2016; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Extracellular levels of glucose impacts epigenomic regulation through O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1.
source: Our findings that extracellular glucose promotes O-GlcNAcylation of DNMT1 and inhibition of DNMT1's function in maintenance of genomic methylation provide direct evidence that extracellular levels of glucose impacts epigenomic regulation.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion drawn from the study's findings.
